title: The good I would (Romans 7:15–25)
hookLine: Paul admits he does what he hates

cards: January first: a resolution on a sticky note. No more scrolling in bed. January third, one in the morning: a phone glowing in the dark, the sticky note still on the mirror.
The gap between what a person means to do and what they actually do is an old one. Paul's letters can sound lofty and sure of themselves. Romans 7 does not.
In it, Paul describes that gap in the first person, with no excuses.

teach.h: THE GOOD WHICH I WILL, I DO NOT.
teach.b: He writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "For that which I work, I understand not. For I do not that good which I will; but the evil which I hate, that I do."

A few lines later, like a man pacing a room: "For the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will not, that I do." Older English put it as the good I would: would in the old sense of what I want, what I will.
He agrees the law is good. He wants the good.

teach.h: A LAW AT WAR IN MY MEMBERS.
teach.b: And something in him pulls the other way: sin dwelling in me, he calls it, a different law at war in his members.
Then the cry: "Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Not a theologian's polished sentence. A groan.
But the very next line answers: "The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord." The Greek reads, thanks be to God. Either way, the answer isn't a better resolution.
It's a person. Honestly, readers have argued for centuries about who the I in this chapter is. Some, including Saint Augustine in his later writings, read it as Paul the believer, still struggling.

teach.h: THE GRACE OF GOD, BY JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: Others read it as Paul looking back at life before Christ, or speaking for humanity in Adam's shoes. The Church hasn't required one reading.

What Catholics do recognize here is what the tradition calls concupiscence: an inclination toward sin that remains even after baptism, not itself sin, but the place where the struggle happens. Paul doesn't hide it.
He names the divided heart, and points to grace.

how: Catholics bring the struggle Paul describes to the sacrament of reconciliation, naming their sins to a priest and receiving absolution, and some make a nightly examination of conscience.

o: poor, with no money or home to go to
miserable, worn down by an inner struggle
wicked, beyond the reach of any help

p: the old word for want or will
the inclination that remains after baptism

s: Paul claims he has stopped struggling with sin
he says the good he wants he doesn't do, and the evil he hates he does.
Christians agree on who the I in Romans 7 is
some read it as a believer's struggle, some as life before Christ, some as humanity in Adam.
Paul's cry is followed at once by an answer
who shall deliver me? the grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord.

games.q: you're writing to a church you've never met, wanting them to trust you. do you admit your own inner struggle?
o: no; present yourself as having it together.
yes; name it plainly, then point to who delivers.
games.why: Paul writes it in the first person: the evil which I hate, that I do. then he names the answer: the grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord.

practice: Name, silently, one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do: just one, no arguing with yourself, no plan yet. Let it be true, the way Paul let it be true on the page; naming it is already different from hiding it.
If you pray, borrow his words, who shall deliver me, and, the grace of God, by Jesus Christ; if not, breathe out and let the honesty be enough.

wordCard.voice: Wretched. Paul's own word for himself in Romans seven, unhappy man that I am, caught between the good he wills and the evil he does. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: wretched, miserable, worn down. unhappy man that I am, in the Douay-Rheims.

carryVoice: Your line: who shall deliver me. Paul's answer was a person, not a plan. See you tomorrow.
